epigraph.text: The credit belongs to the man who is actually in the arena . . . who errs, and comes short again and again, because there is no effort without error and shortcoming.
epigraph.cite: Theodore Roosevelt, “Citizenship in a Republic,” Sorbonne, Paris, 23 April 1910
epigraph._source_record: DOC_BANK/Arena/text/tr-citizenship-in-a-republic-1910.json on Sam's desk. Named public-domain edition: African and European Addresses, ed. Lawrence F. Abbott, 1910. Filed BEFORE the words were used, per canon §6. Sam's own fetch carried the common misquotation (“who neither know victory nor defeat”); the edition reads “who know neither victory nor defeat.” Written from memory it would have shipped wrong past every green gate.
epigraph._gendered_noun: “the man who is actually in the arena” is the 1910 text and is never altered. Sam shipped the full credit line deliberately; BK can swap to “There is no effort without error and shortcoming.” with one word. Both options are on the bank record.

intro: That’s where the name comes from. The person who actually steps into the ring — not the one in the stands with an opinion about it. The one down there gets it wrong, over and over, and gets back up. That’s the only way anybody gets good at anything, and it’s how you’re going to get good at this.

So here’s the deal. Nothing in here is graded. Nothing in here counts against you, ever. This is where you get to be wrong cheaply — as many times as you want — so that when it counts, you’ve already made the mistake and you know what it looks like.
Pick your door. I’ll be with you the whole way.

bowl_only: Welcome back. Your season's right where you left it.
Before you go: new code? Screenshot it or write it down.
welcome_first: Welcome in. Nothing in here is graded. This is where you get better on your own time.
This is practice. Try things, miss some, figure out what you actually know.
Every gauge in here is a skill you'll use long after this class. Start anywhere.
welcome_back: Welcome back. Your season's right where you left it.
Welcome back. Pick a gauge and move the needle.
You came back on your own. That's the habit that makes people good at things.
Welcome back. Every visit is a rep, even a short one.
code_restored: Code worked. Your season's back. Nothing lost.
You saved your code and it paid off. That's planning ahead.
set_complete: That's a set. Every rep builds the skill, right or wrong.
Missed a few? Good. Now you know exactly what to practice.
Most people quit a set when it gets hard. You finished it.
Finished. Take a breath, then decide: same gauge again, or a new one?
The ones you missed are the ones that'll grow you. Go back for them.
set_complete_big: That's a lot of reps in one sitting. That's what getting better looks like.
That's real work today. Your brain earned a break.
attempt_again: Stuck is part of it. Slow down, read the source line first, then take one more swing.
Hard means you're at the edge of what you know. That's exactly where growth happens.
Still stuck? Write down the question and bring it to class. That's not quitting. That's using your resources.
idle_nudge: Still here? One more rep, then call it a day.
No rush. A slow rep still counts.
gauge_up: Your gauge moved. Remember how this felt the first time? That gap is your growth.
Needle's up. You didn't get lucky. You practiced.
That's growth you can see. Keep it moving.
Look at that gauge. Every bit of that, you earned with reps.
goal_prompt: Pick one gauge you want to move before the unit test. Just one. Now go get it.
What's one skill you want to own by Friday? Say it out loud. Goals said out loud get done.
Best version of you, one rep at a time. What's the next one?

HC: A headline with nothing around it is a trap. Context is how you stop getting played.
Before you believe a clip, ask: when, where, and what led to it? That's the skill you just practiced.
Every argument you'll ever have makes more sense once you know what happened first.
TH: Next time somebody says 'trust me,' ask what they're actually claiming. Then ask for proof.
A good thesis is just a clear answer you're willing to defend. Useful in a job interview too.
People who say what they think, clearly, get listened to. That's this skill.
DU: 'The article says' isn't evidence. The exact detail is. Find it, then use it.
Reviews, ads, screenshots, all documents. Somebody made each one for a reason.
Using evidence well is how you win an argument without raising your voice.
EX: Knowing something and explaining it are different skills. The second one gets you hired.
If you can explain it to a friend, you own it.
'Because… which means…' That's the whole skill. It works on anything you're trying to convince someone of.
OE: What you already know is evidence. Don't leave it at the door.
Connecting what you know to what you're reading is how good decisions get made. Anywhere.
CP: Rights, laws, voting: these aren't history. They're the rules you live under right now.
Name the principle out loud. Hinting at it isn't the same as saying it. That's true in an essay and in an argument.
EI: Power, conflict, identity, wealth. They show up in history, and in your group chat, your school and your town.
An enduring issue is a problem people keep having to solve. You'll solve some of them.
Naming the issue is half the skill. Explaining it is the other half: what's the problem, and where do you see it?

habits: Showing up is half of it. The other half is what you do once you're there.
Missed class? This is a good place to catch the skill you missed.
Some days are hard just getting here. You got here. That counts.
Ten minutes of real focus beats an hour of half-attention.
Phone face down for one set. See what happens.
Ten minutes, three times a week, beats two hours the night before. Same with anything you want to get good at.
Ask the question in class. Somebody else is wondering the same thing.
The first ten minutes are where the directions live. Be there for them.
Getting better isn't about finding it easy. It's about being in it.
Lost? Say so early. I can fix confused. I can't fix silent.
A two-line email to a teacher can save you a week of stress.
Say what you need, clearly and politely. Works in school, works at work.
Being right only helps your partner if they can follow you.
Listen first, then answer. It's harder than it sounds and it works everywhere.
Good teammates make the whole group better. That's a skill too.
Bad day? Do one set. Small wins count.
Everybody hits a wall. The ones who get better are the ones who come back.
Asking for help is a skill, not a weakness.
signoff: Good work today. Come back when you're ready.
That's a day. You're a little better than when you walked in.
Before you go: new code? Screenshot it or write it down.
code_new: New code. Screenshot it or write it down. It's your whole season.
Screenshot that code. Future you will thank you.
